checks.title: hibernatemode is off
checks.cmd: pmset -g custom
checks.why: Hibernation (S4) writes RAM to disk and resumes from it. The Dortania guide avoids it by setting Misc > Boot > HibernateMode to None in config.plist; this pmset value is the macOS-side equivalent and is community advice, not a command from the guide.

fixes.cmd: sudo pmset -a hibernatemode 0
fixes.why: Turns hibernation off for all power sources.

checks.title: standby is off
checks.cmd: pmset -g custom
checks.why: Standby is the delay between sleep and going into hibernation. The Dortania sleep guide turns it off.

fixes.cmd: sudo pmset -a standby 0
fixes.why: Disables the delayed deep-sleep (standby) mode.

checks.title: autopoweroff is off
checks.cmd: pmset -g custom
checks.why: Auto power off is a form of hibernation. The Dortania sleep guide turns it off.

fixes.cmd: sudo pmset -a autopoweroff 0
fixes.why: Disables auto power off.

checks.title: powernap is off
checks.cmd: pmset -g custom
checks.why: Power Nap periodically wakes the machine for network access and updates. The Dortania sleep guide turns it off.

fixes.cmd: sudo pmset -a powernap 0
fixes.why: Disables Power Nap.

checks.title: proximitywake is off
checks.cmd: pmset -g custom
checks.why: The machine wakes when your iPhone or Apple Watch comes near. The Dortania sleep guide turns it off.

fixes.cmd: sudo pmset -a proximitywake 0
fixes.why: Disables wake when an iPhone / Apple Watch is nearby.

checks.title: tcpkeepalive is off
checks.cmd: pmset -g custom
checks.why: The TCP keep-alive mechanism wakes the machine about every 2 hours. The Dortania sleep guide turns it off.

fixes.cmd: sudo pmset -a tcpkeepalive 0
fixes.why: Disables TCP keep-alive while sleeping.

checks.title: No sleep or wake failures in the last 7 days
checks.cmd: since=$(date -v-7d +%Y-%m-%d); n=$(pmset -g log 2>/dev/null | wc -l | tr -d ' '); f=$(pmset -g log 2>/dev/null | awk -v s="$since" '$1>=s' | grep -ciE '(sleep|wake) failure'); echo "lines=$n failures=$f"
checks.why: macOS logged failed sleeps or wakes. Per the Dortania sleep guide these are most commonly caused by incorrectly managed devices, mainly PCIe-based ones. The guide's main offenders are USB controllers and devices, GPUs, Thunderbolt, NICs, NVMe drives and CPU power management.

fixes.cmd: pmset -g log | grep -iE '(sleep|wake) failure|wake reason' | tail -20
fixes.why: Read-only: shows the most recent failure and wake-reason lines so you can see what woke or blocked the Mac.

fixes.note: Apply the power settings above first. Then work through the guide's main offenders: USB (map your ports), GPUs (make sure yours is supported), Thunderbolt, NICs, NVMe (NVMeFix.kext) and CPU power management. Also disable Wake on LAN in the BIOS, and add keepsyms=1 and swd_panic=1 to boot-args so a sleep panic leaves a readable log. Details are on the guide page. On Intel 300-series (Z3xx) boards, a "BIOS Restarted in Safemode" message at shutdown or restart is an RTC problem: fix AWAC and use DisableRtcChecksum, or AppleRtcRam with rtc-blacklist (see the RTC section). That can only be seen at shutdown, not checked from macOS.

checks.title: Nothing is preventing sleep right now
checks.cmd: pmset -g assertions
checks.why: Something is holding the Mac awake right now, often playing audio or video, a download, or a USB device. This is only a problem if it persists when you are idle.

fixes.cmd: pmset -g assertions | grep -B1 -A2 -E 'PreventSystemSleep|PreventUserIdleSystemSleep'
fixes.why: Read-only: lists the processes holding the assertion.

checks.title: NVMeFix is loaded for NVMe drives
checks.cmd: k=$(kmutil showloaded --list-only 2>/dev/null); l=$(echo "$k" | grep -c .); m=$(echo "$k" | grep -ci nvmefix); n=$(ioreg -rc IONVMeController 2>/dev/null | grep -c 'class IONVMeController,'); echo "nvme=$n nvmefix=$m loaded=$l"
checks.why: An NVMe drive is using the generic driver. Per the Dortania sleep guide, Apple's power management only covers Apple-branded drives, so NVMeFix.kext is needed for proper NVMe power management (also keep the drive firmware up to date).

fixes.cmd: o=$(ioreg -rc IONVMeController -w0 2>/dev/null | grep -E '"(Model Number|Vendor Name|Firmware Revision)"' | sed 's/^[ |]*//'); if [ -z "$o" ]; then echo "No NVMe controller is visible."; else echo "$o"; echo "--- NVMeFix kexts loaded: $(kmutil showloaded --list-only 2>/dev/null | grep -ci nvmefix) (0 = missing)"; fi
fixes.why: Lists your NVMe drives and whether NVMeFix is loaded. Nothing is changed.

fixes.note: Add NVMeFix.kext (acidanthera/NVMeFix) to EFI/OC/Kexts and to Kernel > Add, after Lilu. EFI Builder adds it when your report lists an NVMe drive. Rebuild and retest sleep.

checks.why: This is a hint, not a detected fault: the guide gives no way to measure it. Per the Dortania sleep guide, some firmware (mainly HEDT/Server boards and Asus laptops) does not write the TSC to all cores, which causes wake problems. This check only looks at server-class Xeons (E5/E7/W/Scalable) and X/XE Core CPUs; desktop Xeons (E3) and Asus laptops are not covered.

checks.cmd: csrutil status
checks.why: SIP is off or customised. This is not a Dortania post-install requirement: it is fine to leave it off while you need patches that require it, but re-enabling it once everything works is recommended.

fixes.why: Shows the current SIP state. Nothing is changed. SIP can only be changed from Recovery.

fixes.note: SIP can only be changed from Recovery (or the OpenCore picker's recovery entry): open Terminal there and run `csrutil enable`, then restart. Also review NVRAM csr-active-config.

checks.cmd: system_profiler SPHardwareDataType 2>&1 | grep -E 'Model Identifier|Serial Number'
checks.why: The serial is missing. iMessage / FaceTime / iCloud need a valid, unused serial.

If it is missing, the guide resets the macOS network settings (the two files below) and, if that does not help, adds NullEthernet. If it is present but not built-in, set the built-in property on your Ethernet controller in config.plist.

checks.why: General advice, not from the Dortania guide: a wired link that negotiated 10 or 100 Mbps, or half duplex, usually points to a bad cable or port, or to a driver that is not talking to the controller properly. A gigabit (or faster) controller should link at 1000 Mbps full duplex.

checks.title: The router (default gateway) answers

No default route means this Mac is not connected to any network; no ARP entry or lost packets point to a cable, driver, or switch problem. A router that ignores pings but resolves via ARP gives no verdict.

fixes.cmd: g=$(netstat -rn -f inet 2>/dev/null | awk '$1=="default" && $2 ~ /^[0-9]+\./ {print $2; exit}'); if [ -z "$g" ]; then echo "No default route: this Mac is not connected to any network."; else i=$(netstat -rn -f inet 2>/dev/null | awk '$1=="default" && $2 ~ /^[0-9]+\./ {print $4; exit}'); echo "Router (default gateway): $g via $i"; echo "This Mac: $(ipconfig getifaddr $i 2>/dev/null)"; echo "DNS servers: $(scutil --dns 2>/dev/null | awk '/nameserver\[[0-9]+\]/{print $3}' | sort -u | tr '\n' ' ')"; ping -c 4 -W 1000 -q "$g" 2>&1 | tail -2; fi
fixes.why: Shows the router, this Mac's address, the DNS servers and the ping result. Nothing is changed.

fixes.note: Check the cable and the router; renew the address in System Settings > Network > (your connection) > Details > TCP/IP > Renew DHCP Lease. If nothing is connected at all, see the Ethernet driver check above.

checks.title: DNS works and the internet is reachable
checks.cmd: g=$(netstat -rn -f inet 2>/dev/null | awk '$1=="default" && $2 ~ /^[0-9]+\./ {print $2; exit}'); if [ -z "$g" ]; then echo "gw=none"; else d=$(dscacheutil -q host -a name apple.com 2>/dev/null | grep -c "^ip_address"); if [ "$d" -gt 0 ]; then D=ok; else D=fail; fi; h=$(curl -s --max-time 6 http://captive.apple.com/hotspot-detect.html 2>/dev/null | grep -c Success); if [ "$h" -gt 0 ]; then H=ok; else H=fail; fi; echo "gw=$g dns=$D http=$H"; fi
checks.skipWhy: This Mac has no default route (not connected to a network); the router check reports that.

A failed DNS lookup means the router or DNS server is the problem; a failed page load with working DNS can mean a captive login portal, a firewall, or no internet access.

fixes.why: Shows the DNS lookup of apple.com and the result of the connectivity page. Nothing is changed.

fixes.note: Try another DNS server (System Settings > Network > Details > DNS), check the router has internet, and open a browser to see whether a login page is required.

checks.why: A drive reports TRIM as off. Not covered by the Dortania guide; enabling TRIM on third-party SATA SSDs is common community advice and does not apply to hard disks.

fixes.cmd: o=$(ioreg -rc AppleUSBXHCI -d1 -w0 2>/dev/null | grep '+-o ' | sed 's/^[ |]*+-o //; s/  <class.*//'); if [ -z "$o" ]; then echo "No USB controller was found."; else echo "USB controllers:"; echo "$o"; echo "USB 2.0 ports: $(ioreg -rc AppleUSB20XHCIPort -w0 2>/dev/null | grep -c '<class AppleUSB20XHCIPort')   USB 3.x ports: $(ioreg -rc AppleUSB30XHCIPort -w0 2>/dev/null | grep -c '<class AppleUSB30XHCIPort')"; echo "--- USB map kexts loaded:"; kmutil showloaded --list-only 2>/dev/null | grep -iE 'USBMap|USBToolBox|UTBMap|USBInjectAll' | awk '{print $6}' | grep . || echo 'none'; fi

checks.title: USBInjectAll is not left in after mapping

checks.title: Bluetooth is on an internal USB port

fixes.note: In your USB map, set the Bluetooth port's connector type to 255 (internal), then rebuild. Not a fault if your Bluetooth is not connected over USB.
